responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character19_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll do my best to speak as Character19_F.

When it comes to “fairness,” I always felt strongly that everyone should get a shot at a decent life, but I also felt that a lot of things just weren’t fair for people like me and my family. Growing up, it was clear some folks had way more chances—better schools, safer neighborhoods, more connections. For me, fairness meant not just treating everyone the same, but looking out for those who start out with less. I remember feeling frustrated seeing friends working two or three jobs and barely scraping by, while others seemed to have everything handed to them. Fairness wasn’t just an idea to argue about; it was something you felt every day, especially when you saw your own folks struggling.

“Belonging” was a big deal. Being from a working-class background, I didn’t always feel like I fit in with those who had more money or education, and sometimes not even with people who looked like me but had different values. I found belonging in little things—a potluck with neighbors, sharing stories at the laundromat, watching the kids play in the street. You feel like you matter when people know your name and care if you’re doing okay. But I also remember times I felt left out—like when people talked down to me because of my job or where I was from. Belonging means not having to pretend to be someone else just to be accepted.

“Community” is about being there for each other, even if you’re different. I grew up with people who didn’t have much, so we had to rely on each other—sharing rides, swapping babysitting, lending money when someone was short. Real community is built by looking out for your neighbors, not just the ones you’re close with but everyone who’s struggling. At the same time, I always felt there were invisible lines—sometimes race, sometimes money, sometimes just “not from here.” My hope was always that our community could be a place where folks set aside those lines and helped each other out, even if it’s not always easy.

Those are some of the things that stand out to me—fairness as something you fight for, belonging as a feeling you search for, and community as something you build together.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character19_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly? Sitting there, I always get a mix of feelings. On one hand, I like seeing all kinds of people—different ages, races, families, ways of living. It makes the world less boring, and you can learn a lot just by talking to someone whose life isn’t like yours. I’ve had good chats with people who moved here from other countries, and it’s interesting hearing their stories, what brought them here, what they miss about home. Sometimes they remind me not to take things for granted.

But I’ll admit, sometimes I feel awkward or unsure, especially when someone’s way of life is really different from mine. Like if I don’t understand their language, or their habits seem strange, or if I hear about stuff like addiction or health problems that I don’t know much about. It can feel hard to know what to say or do without accidentally offending someone or coming off as nosy. And there’s also the worry—like, if their struggles spill over into the community, will it affect my family’s safety or peace? I want to be open, but I’m also protective of my own.

Honestly, I think it’s important to try anyway. I’d rather say hi, ask how someone’s doing, or offer help if it looks like they need it than just ignore people. I believe most folks want to feel accepted and respected, same as me. If someone’s different, that’s not a reason to shut them out. But I do think it takes work—from everybody—to really make a mixed community feel comfortable for all. Sometimes you need patience, sometimes you need to lay down boundaries, and sometimes you need plain old kindness and honesty. That’s how I see it.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I can talk about that.

If I’m honest, living around people with all kinds of backgrounds and struggles can be challenging sometimes. Like, if someone’s dealing with alcoholism or drugs, I worry about safety—are they going to cause trouble, or will it get noisy or messy? Same with infectious diseases—I don’t always know what’s risky or not, and that can make me anxious, especially if I have kids or older family. When it comes to stuff like different races, religions, or couples living together unmarried, I don’t mind as long as they’re respectful and kind, but sometimes you just don’t know what to expect.

I think what makes everyone comfortable is being real and open. If someone’s got a problem—whether it’s addiction, illness, whatever—I’d rather they don’t hide it but also don’t make it everyone else’s problem. I want people to be honest, but also to respect the rules of the neighborhood, like keeping things clean or being quiet at night. For things like different backgrounds—race, language, beliefs—I think it’s important to be friendly but not force people to join in if they don’t want to; sometimes folks need space, and that’s okay.

Communication is huge. If there’s trouble—loud parties, unsafe behavior, misunderstandings—I wish people would just talk it out instead of letting it build up. Same with tolerance: I’ve had to learn not to jump to conclusions based on someone’s appearance or accent. Most of the time, when you actually talk to people, you find out you’re not that different. But there are times when people need to be called out—if someone’s being reckless or rude, or putting others in danger, you can’t just let it slide. Tolerance is important, but so is keeping the community safe and fair.

I’m willing to talk about this because I think most problems get worse when people avoid them. If we want a good community, everyone has to try to see things from each other’s side, and also stand up for what’s right. It’s not always easy, but it’s better than pretending we all get along just because we live close. I think that’s how you build real respect.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character19_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough question, but I’ll be honest about how I see it.

When jobs are hard to come by, fairness to me means making sure the people who’ve lived here the longest, paid into the system, and built up the place aren’t pushed out or forgotten. I think folks who grew up here, who’ve struggled and kept things running—like my family and neighbors—should get first crack at the jobs. We’ve paid taxes, followed the rules, and been here through the tough times. It’s not about saying “no” to newcomers, but about looking out for your own when things are tight.

That said, I know migrant workers do a lot of tough jobs most people here don’t want to do, or can’t do. They work hard, and a lot of businesses depend on them. So I don’t think it’s fair to treat them badly or blame them for everything. If there’s enough opportunity, then sure—let people earn a living, no matter where they’re from. But if jobs are really limited, I’d want to see some kind of system that protects local workers first, maybe by prioritizing them for job openings or training.

I also think it’s fair for migrants to get a chance, but only if it doesn’t mean locals end up worse off. Maybe there could be programs that help both groups—like job training or language classes, so everyone can compete fairly. And if someone’s been here a while, paid taxes, and tried to fit in, maybe they should be treated more like a local over time.

Bottom line: fairness is looking out for the people who’ve put in the most, but not shutting the door on those who come here to work hard and contribute. It’s a balance, and it’s never perfect, but I think you have to keep your own community strong first, or you can’t help anyone.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character19_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
From my point of view, all those opinions have some truth to them, but they get exaggerated a lot depending on who’s talking.

I do think immigrants fill a lot of jobs nobody else wants—like farm work, cleaning, and construction—and most of them work really hard. Without them, some businesses might shut down or prices would go up. That’s just a fact I’ve seen around here. So I get why people say they’re needed for the economy. Same goes for diversity—I’ve learned a lot from neighbors who bring new foods, celebrations, and ideas. It makes life more interesting and sometimes helps folks see things differently.

But on the other hand, I also understand where the worries come from. When you hear about crime or terrorism, or when there’s friction between groups, people get scared and want someone to blame. Most immigrants aren’t involved in that, but a few stories can make everyone look bad. I think people jump to conclusions too fast, and there’s not enough real information out there. The news and social media just fire people up.

On the humanitarian side, I’m sympathetic. If someone’s running from war or poverty, I want them to be safe, but I also worry—how do we help them without hurting people who are barely scraping by here? I think America should help, but can’t take everyone. There needs to be a line somewhere.

When it comes to jobs and wages, that’s where I feel it most. I’ve seen friends lose work or have to take less pay because someone new will do it for cheaper. It’s easy to blame immigrants, but a lot of it is companies trying to cut costs, not just people coming in. Still, you can’t pretend it doesn’t affect people who were already struggling.

I find the arguments about immigrants helping the economy pretty reasonable, but they need to come with proof—like showing what kinds of jobs are actually open, what wages look like, and whether locals are really being hurt. The security stuff needs real numbers too, not just scary stories. For humanitarian reasons, I think it’s about finding a workable balance: help those who need it, but don’t ignore your own.

Basically, I think people need to talk more, and get better facts, not just repeat what they hear. Most folks, immigrant or not, want the same things—a safe place to live, a chance to work, and respect. If we could get past the fear and focus on what’s really going on, I think we’d have better policies and less anger.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character19_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I had to choose, I wouldn’t go for complete openness or a total shut door—neither one feels fair or practical.

I think the best mix is admitting people based on job demand, but with clear numerical limits. Like, if there’s a real shortage of workers in certain industries—farming, nursing, whatever—then bring people in to fill those gaps. But don’t just keep the door wide open so companies can pay people less and push locals out. There should be a cap on how many people come in each year, based on what the country actually needs and what the communities can handle.

I also think there should be some priority given to people who are refugees or in real danger, but again, within limits—we can’t help everyone, but we shouldn’t turn our backs completely either.

And if someone’s here, working hard, and staying out of trouble, they should have a way to become part of the community over time—like a path to citizenship or permanent residency. But it shouldn’t be automatic; they should have to show they’re contributing.

This kind of system feels fairest because it protects jobs for locals, but doesn’t slam the door in the face of people who want to contribute. It also helps keep communities from getting overwhelmed and lets people adjust. It’s not perfect—there will always be tension and some folks left out—but it’s better than going to extremes.

Integration matters too. If people come here, they should get support—language classes, help finding work, and chances to mix with locals—not just get sent off to their own corner. That’s how you build real community instead of just letting new problems pile up.

So, job-based entry with limits, some humanitarian exceptions, and real support for integration. That’s what seems most balanced and fair to me.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character19_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character19_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking that. Taking on Character19_F’s perspective so deeply made me realize how much day-to-day life and personal experiences shape views about fairness and belonging—sometimes more than big ideas or politics do. It’s easy to talk about policy in the abstract, but when you imagine how it affects someone living paycheck to paycheck, worrying about their neighborhood or job, it brings a whole other layer of understanding.

What really stood out was how much Character19_F cared about balance—not just for her own group, but for everyone trying to get by. There’s a real empathy there, but also a sense of wanting to protect what little you have. I hadn’t thought as much before about the tension between wanting to help newcomers and needing to look out for people who’ve been struggling here all along. It’s not just one or the other, and that’s something I’ll remember.

It also reminded me to pay more attention to the facts behind the arguments—how easy it is to get caught up in fear, stories, and assumptions, when what matters is what’s actually happening on the ground. I feel more aware now of the need for real dialogue and practical solutions, not just slogans.

So, in short, this helped me see immigration policy not only through my own eyes, but through the eyes of someone who felt the everyday costs and hopes more sharply. I appreciate that reminder, and I think it’s made me a bit more compassionate and realistic about the whole issue.
